passages.text: Double descent has sparked considerable interest, with recent work relating it to the data, the model and the learning configuration. Practical fine-tuning commonly involves training a small adapter on top of frozen pretrained weights, as in low-rank adaptation (LoRA). The adapter’s rank is the hyperparameter that sets its capacity, yet how this rank relates to double descent has not been well explored. We quantify this relation under label noise on four vision backbones and a 7 7 B language model with a module-matched rank sweep (MMRS), which extends past full rank and compares every rank with dense fine-tuning of the same modules, paired by seed. On DeiT-Tiny, risk is lowest at rank one and rises sharply as the adapter becomes able to fit the noisy labels, forming an interpolation cliff. Past the peak, risk falls again, but every tested post-peak rank that still saves parameters remains above dense risk. Rank-one LoRA outperforms dense fine-tuning on three of the four vision backbones, consistent with strong regularization at small rank. LoRA thus exhibits a second descent, but matches dense risk only after losing its parameter advantage, first on DeiT-Tiny at four times dense’s projection weights. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/lora-second-descent-C7B5 .

passages.text: Deep research agents answer complex questions through repeated search. They rely on a harness that runs their tool calls and returns evidence to their context. This creates a trade-off: Search works best over long passages, which give enough context for reliable semantic matching. But the returned evidence should be short, because every observation stays in the agent’s context for the rest of the trajectory. We introduce CORE , a training-free harness that combines coarse-to-fine search with context management. CORE retrieves passages with a dense retriever. It then reuses the token-level similarities from a late-interaction reranker to return only the most relevant snippet from each passage. Context management lets the agent expand the context around sources it has already retrieved and suppresses repeated snippets. In controlled closed-search comparisons with the Tongyi DeepResearch and OpenResearcher harnesses, CORE achieves state-of-the-art answer accuracy and evidence recall across three agent models and three benchmarks (BrowseComp-Plus, BrowseComp-Wikipedia and BrowseComp-Plus CM ), on corpora containing up to 553M documents.

The key idea of our CORE, a co arse-to-fine deep re search harness, is to shift this burden from the agent to the search itself: relevant text is found by searching over broad passages, while the agent receives only concise snippets. We organize the search space into documents, passages, segments, and snippets, and treat evidence as the text admitted into the agent’s context to serve the local goal of a sub-query or the global goal of the question. CORE’s search tool first performs coarse retrieval of passages with a reasoning-aware dense retriever ( Chen et al., 2026b ) , then fine-grained reranking with a late-interaction model ( Khattab and Zaharia, 2020 ; Chaffin, 2025 ) , whose token-level similarities also locate the most relevant snippet within each passage at no additional encoding cost. CORE’s context manager lets the agent expand the context around previously retrieved sources and deduplicates snippets across searches. Our contributions are as follows: • Coarse-to-fine search. CORE searches at the passage level but returns evidence at the snippet level. It reuses the token-level similarities computed during late-interaction reranking to locate the most relevant snippet in each passage, without any additional encoding. • A training-free harness. CORE combines coarse-to-fine search with context management and works with any agent model without retraining. Context management offsets the narrowness of snippet-level evidence by letting the agent expand the context around previously retrieved sources, and it suppresses snippets repeated across searches.

• State-of-the-art closed-search results at scale. To ensure reproducibility, we restrict the study to closed search over fixed corpora. Across three agent models, CORE achieves the highest accuracy and evidence recall in every model–benchmark comparison, setting new state-of-the-art results to the best of our knowledge.

passages.text: Modern LLM optimizers such as Muon often produce weight matrices with higher effective rank than Adam, yet further spectral control has delivered only modest gains. We identify a tension behind this result: concentrated spectra can suppress gradient directions in coupled weight matrices and slow optimization, while constraints maintained throughout training can limit task-specific adaptation and raise the attainable loss floor. We introduce ORCA (Orthogonal Regularization, Cooled After), a minimal optimizer intervention that applies strong but temporary soft orthogonality regularization early in training, then removes it. This allows the weights to benefit from a broader spectrum early on and adapt freely afterward. Across LLaMA, Qwen3, and fine-grained mixture-of-experts models ranging from 130M to 8B parameters, ORCA achieves lower final validation loss than Muon. Its loss reduction relative to Muon matches or exceeds Muon’s reduction relative to Adam. Ablations support the early-shaping, later-release design. Further, ORCA requires no architectural changes and adds minimal overhead. An implementation is available at https://github.com/uuurraaa/ORCA_Optimizer .

However, we argue that this trade-off is not fundamental. Spectral regularization may be most valuable early, when it can shape the optimization trajectory, yet become a liability if maintained as the weights adapt to the task. The two effects need not be accepted together: we can use the constraint to shape the spectrum, then release it before it restricts the final solution. This motivates a minimal method ORCA (Orthogonal Regularization, Cooled After): During an initial phase, ORCA applies a soft orthogonality penalty, R orth ​ ( 𝐖 ) = 1 4 ​ ‖ 𝐖𝐖 ⊤ − 𝐈 ‖ F 2 R_{\mathrm{orth}}(\mathbf{W})=\frac{1}{4}\|\mathbf{W}\mathbf{W}^{\top}-\mathbf{I}\|_{F}^{2} . Then directly removes it at a single switch point. Training thereafter follows the standard optimizer update, with no gradual decay or further changes. This design lets early regularization influence the optimization path without prescribing the spectrum throughout training. In our experiments, this simple release is followed by faster loss reduction and a lower final validation loss than Muon. Figure 1.1: LLaMA 130M training dynamics. Effective rank is measured on a middle-layer V V projection; the dashed line marks regularization release. Figure 1.1 illustrates the transition. While the penalty is active, the effective rank of the weight matrix rises sharply above Muon’s, although ORCA initially has a higher validation loss. After release, the rank falls from its peak but remains above Muon’s, while validation loss decreases rapidly, crosses the Muon curve. The result is consistent with early spectral shaping leaving a useful effect on the subsequent trajectory, even after the explicit penalty is gone. Controlled interventions in Section 5 further investigates into this connection.

We evaluate ORCA on LLaMA, Qwen3, and fine-grained MoE models ranging from 130M to 8B parameters, including 100B-token training runs. ORCA achieves lower final validation loss than Muon across these settings. In most experiments, the reduction is 0.02–0.04, comparable to or greater than Muon’s gain over Adam. To put this loss reduction in perspective, on LLaMA 1.3B, ORCA achieving the 0.024 lower validation loss reaches Muon’s 100k-step loss in just 60k steps. Further, downstream evaluations, alternative early spectral interventions, multi-seed runs, and ablations of method parameters and intervention timing further support these gains. Together, these results show that early spectral shaping followed by constraint relaxation can improve training efficiency and final performance across architectures without substantial changes to the optimizer. To summarize the contributions of the paper: (1) We illustrate a trade-off in spectral control through a simplified model and empirical observations: favorable spectra can accelerate optimization but persistent constraints may harm the attainable solution quality. (2) We introduce ORCA, a minimal shape-then-release optimizer that leverages early orthogonal regularization to improve optimization trajectories while allowing unconstrained adaptation in later training. (3) We demonstrate ORCA’s effectiveness across diverse LLM architectures and scales, achieving faster convergence and lower loss than existing optimizers. Through extensive controlled experiments, we further validate the mechanism that early effective-rank shaping drives the observed improvements.

We also evaluate how the optimization performance translates into token efficiency by measuring the training required to reach a common target loss. We continued ORCA from its original 51k-step checkpoint, starting the final decay early, and reached a validation loss of 2.318 at approximately 60k steps. The standard Muon run, using its original 100k-step settings, reached the same loss at 100k steps ( Figure 2(a) ). Therefore, ORCA used 40% fewer tokens to reach this target, a 1.66× token-efficiency gain. To save compute, we reused the checkpoint without retuning ORCA for the shorter run: its original 25k-step shaping stage accounts for 41.7% of the 60k-step budget rather than the tuned default of 25%. Pruning is a natural approach to this problem, but practical gains depend on the sparsity structure: unstructured sparsity often requires specialized kernels or hardware, whereas structured pruning removes entire computational units and translates directly into efficiency gains ( Wen et al., 2016 ; An et al., 2024 ) . Feed-forward modules can account for roughly two thirds of Transformer parameters ( Geva et al., 2021 ) , making their hidden channels a natural target for structured compression. Global pruning ranks channels across layers jointly, allowing different layers to retain different numbers of channels ( Lee et al., 2021 ; An et al., 2024 ) . Post-pruning fine-tuning adds computational cost, especially for large models ( Kwon et al., 2022 ; Sun et al., 2024 ) , motivating compressibility to emerge during training so that pruning requires little or no recovery. Muon has demonstrated strong training efficiency across model scales, from small vision and language-model benchmarks to billion-parameter language models ( Jordan et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025 ; Shah et al., 2025 ) . Its matrix update can be viewed as a linear minimization oracle over a spectral-norm ball, giving Muon a steepest-descent interpretation in spectral-norm geometry ( Pethick et al., 2025 ) . Prior work has shown that implicit bias can depend on optimization geometry ( Gunasekar et al., 2018 ) . For Muon, recent theory identifies a spectral-norm margin bias in linear and smooth homogeneous models ( Fan et al., 2025 ; Gronich and Vardi, 2026 ) . Yet we find that Muon-trained Transformers degrade rapidly under structured MLP pruning, suggesting that Muon’s spectral geometry does not by itself encourage structured compressibility. As shown in Figure 1 , a Muon-trained ViT-S/16 on ImageNet-1K collapses after only 30 % 30\% global MLP channel pruning, with Top-1 accuracy falling from 75.23 % 75.23\% to 3.17 % 3.17\% . In contrast, our proposed Budget Muon (BMuon) algorithm retains 74.08 % 74.08\% Top-1 accuracy after 70 % 70\% pruning, nearly matching its 74.17 % 74.17\% accuracy before pruning, with no post-pruning recovery. This raises the central question: can Muon’s spectral geometry be modified to encourage structured compressibility?

For a fixed allocation, BMuon introduces a diagonal reweighting inside Muon’s spectral-norm constraint, with the components of the update variable corresponding to channel j j in block ℓ \ell weighted according to its allocation μ j ℓ \mu_{j}^{\ell} . passages.text: Finding a paper from an informal research idea requires more than matching topic words: relevant work may use different terminology, and its distinguishing mechanism may be absent from the abstract. We present Idea2Prior, an auditable literature-search system built on PaperArena. It combines multi-source discovery, identity verification, facet-based abstract assessment, semantic citation expansion, and joint Expert ranking. A retrieval-only mode ranks up to five papers from a shortlist of at most 60, using complete available abstracts and locally selected PDF evidence from five fixed acquisition attempts, without generating a long-form report. In a historical comparison covering ten queries from each of EASY, MEDIUM, and HARD, aggregate reported Hit@5 is 53.3% for Idea2Prior, 43.3% for ChatGPT web Deep Research, and 36.7% for Gemini web Deep Research under the documented accounting convention. The advantage is concentrated in EASY and MEDIUM; ChatGPT leads on HARD. Selected Idea2Prior runs average 8 minutes 53 seconds, compared with user-reported web averages of 5.2 and 4.7 minutes. A separate nine-query API sample averages $0.0945 per task; this is a historical cost observation, not a matched comparison with web subscription costs. Pairwise Top 5 coverage ranges from 6% to 34%, showing differing returned evidence sets. The system also exposes optional implementation analysis and citation-evolution tools. These results support targeted idea-to-paper retrieval while leaving general web research, forum search, and broader relevance evaluation open.

Researchers often remember an idea before they remember a title: a neighborhood with uncertain boundaries, a circuit transformation with a particular constraint, or an assistant that recognizes when a complex task changes. Recovering relevant prior work from such descriptions is difficult because vocabulary, application setting, and the level of technical detail can differ substantially between a query and a paper. A useful assistant must retrieve candidates, establish their bibliographic identities, and distinguish a close conceptual match from work that merely shares a topic. LLM-based research systems provide useful ways to explore and synthesize sources. STORM organizes research into multi-perspective information gathering and article outlining [ 3 ] , Co-STORM supports interactive exploration [ 4 ] , and Agent Laboratory connects literature review with experimentation and reporting [ 5 ] . Our focus is narrower: given an idea, which five identifiable papers are most likely to match it, and what evidence explains their selection? This objective is not equivalent to the quality of a general research report. We introduce Idea2Prior, an extension of PaperArena and its implementation [ 1 , 2 ] . The contribution is an engineering and evaluation framework for inspectable idea-to-paper retrieval: it preserves search queries, candidate identities, assessments, filtering reasons, PDF availability, and the final ranking. This makes it possible to distinguish a discovery miss from a candidate that was retrieved but lost during filtering, or from a task that failed operationally. A high-level result alone cannot make those distinctions.

The central design separates inexpensive assessment of a broad candidate pool from a bounded examination of document evidence. After abstract assessment and citation expansion, an Expert model jointly considers up to 60 candidates. Five papers are selected for PDF acquisition; unavailable PDFs are not replaced by additional papers in retrieval-only mode. Complete available abstracts remain in the Expert input, along with evidence availability and up to six locally selected PDF passages per acquired paper. A missing PDF does not make a paper irrelevant and does not prevent it from ranking first. The optional full-report mode retains downstream synthesis for users who need a written literature analysis. The revised evaluation covers 30 query cases: ten from each of three prompt tiers, with shared targets across tiers. The reported aggregate Hit@5 is 16/30 for Idea2Prior, 13/30 for ChatGPT web Deep Research, and 11/30 for Gemini web Deep Research. The ChatGPT total includes one convention-based credit, disclosed in Section 5.1 . Idea2Prior leads both baselines by 20 percentage points on EASY and MEDIUM, but trails ChatGPT by 10 points on HARD. Mean selected-run latency is 8.89 minutes, and a separately reported nine-query cost sample averages $0.0945. Thus the present evidence shows a recovery advantage in two tiers and a low observed API cost, with longer latency than the supplied browser averages. Our contributions are: 1. An auditable retrieval-and-ranking workflow with identity-aware candidate records, semantic citation filtering, and a joint Top 5 decision over a bounded shortlist.

The released benchmark contains 30 queries in each of EASY, MEDIUM, and HARD. According to the dataset construction record, GPT-6 Astra in ChatGPT was used to extract and generate the shared literature-search prompts. EASY supplies more identifying detail, MEDIUM removes some detail, and HARD uses shorter, less specific descriptions. These are intended difficulty levels rather than independently calibrated labels. The tiers are not independent paper pools; in particular, MEDIUM and HARD share targets with different wording. The present comparison uses the first ten IDs of each tier: EASY N001–N010, MEDIUM C001–C010, and HARD C001–C010. Each system receives the same filled item prompt: a paper-finding instruction, the 2015–2025 publication/verified-version constraint, up-to-five distinct works with exact bibliographic fields and a short match explanation, identity verification and deduplication requirements, and the idea text. The designated target is not supplied to retrieval. Original prompts and outputs are preserved; Appendix A gives the exact shared wrappers and a three-tier example. These are retrieval prompts, distinct from the internal scoring prompts. ChatGPT and Gemini were tested through their October 2026 web Deep Research interfaces; backend model/build identifiers and subscription tiers were not recorded. Idea2Prior used its API pipeline. Preserved Expert outputs identify the configured alias openai/gemini-3.8-flash ; a compatibility-protocol alias does not independently verify the upstream served model. The released native-Gemini preset is not a newly benchmarked replacement for those historical runs.

Results use final selected runs, including authorized replacements of operationally failed attempts. They therefore measure selected-result recovery, not first-attempt reliability. EASY initially produced five target hits over ten planned queries before recovery; the final selection produced nine. We retain the historical ChatGPT EASY convention of 7/10: six observed hits plus one convention-based counted hit. No returned paper or intersection is fabricated for that credit. Counting only observed hits would make ChatGPT EASY 6/10 and aggregate recovery 12/30; our primary table preserves the earlier agreed convention explicitly. These browser outputs also carry a control limitation: new conversations were used, but the operator reported ChatGPT memory/history references enabled during earlier testing. The adopted HARD comparison uses the replacement NEW report. This historical record does not establish a newly controlled, contamination-free evaluation. Future comparisons should use isolated sessions with memory disabled and a frozen protocol.

Many LoRA variants improve the initialization or optimization of low-rank factors. At each training step, however, their first-order weight-space directions are constrained by the current parameterization. We characterize the corresponding LoRA-accessible gradient space and show that it coincides with the tangent space induced by the current LoRA parameterization. This characterization yields an orthogonal decomposition of the full weight gradient at the current model parameters. We term the component orthogonal to this space the normal gradient . Based on this decomposition, we propose GDLoRA (Gradient-Decomposed Low-Rank Adaptation) . GDLoRA reconstructs the full weight gradient from forward activations and backward signals, extracts its normal component, and directly updates the base weights with this component, while retaining standard AdamW optimization for the LoRA factors. GDLoRA incorporates complementary normal gradients without increasing standard LoRA’s optimizer-state memory budget under matched adapter and optimizer configurations. Experiments on natural language understanding, mathematical reasoning, commonsense reasoning, and image classification show that GDLoRA consistently improves over LoRA and narrows the performance gap to FFT. The code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/GDLoRA .

Large foundation models achieve strong performance across diverse applications ( Devlin et al., 2019 ; Brown et al., 2020 ; Chowdhery et al., 2023 ) , but adapting them through full fine-tuning (FFT) incurs substantial computation and memory costs for gradients and optimizer states ( Rajbhandari et al., 2020 ) . Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) reduces these costs by optimizing a small subset of parameters while keeping most pretrained weights frozen ( Houlsby et al., 2019 ; Li and Liang, 2021 ; Lester et al., 2021 ) . Among these methods, Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) ( Hu et al., 2021 ) introduces trainable low-rank factors into pretrained layers, reducing optimizer-state memory while maintaining competitive downstream performance.

Despite these advantages, a performance gap can remain between LoRA and FFT. A related line of research seeks to enable full-rank training with reduced optimizer-state memory. Fira ( Chen et al., 2024 ) pursues this goal by combining adaptive optimization of low-rank projected gradients with scaled residual updates. Its projection bases are obtained through SVD and reused across multiple optimization steps to amortize decomposition costs. However, as the leading gradient subspace drifts during training, reused bases may become less aligned with important directions of subsequent gradients, potentially limiting the effectiveness of adaptive optimization, while more frequent basis refreshes incur additional computational costs. A detailed analysis is provided in Appendix A . Another line of research improves LoRA optimization through adapter initialization and gradient alignment. LoRA-GA ( Wang et al., 2024 ) uses full-gradient information to initialize the factors so that their initial induced weight-space gradient better approximates that of full fine-tuning. LoRA-Pro ( Wang et al., 2025 ) studies the equivalent weight-space gradient induced by the adapter gradients and adjusts them to improve its approximation to the full weight gradient.

Based on this decomposition, we propose GDLoRA (Gradient-Decomposed Low-Rank Adaptation) . GDLoRA reconstructs the full weight gradient of LoRA-injected layers from forward activations and backward signals, normalizes the recovered gradient by the number of input positions, and extracts its normal component using the current LoRA tangent space. This additional token-count normalization applies only to the normal branch and preserves the gradient direction. The adapter parameters follow standard AdamW optimization, while the token-normalized normal gradient directly updates the base weights initialized from the pretrained model. Both branches use quantities computed from the same pre-update parameters. The normal branch introduces no additional momentum or variance buffers for the base weights. In this way, GDLoRA approaches or matches the performance of full fine-tuning in the evaluated settings, without introducing additional optimizer-state memory overhead relative to standard LoRA under matched adapter and optimizer configurations. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We characterize the LoRA-accessible gradient space through its equivalence to the tangent space induced by the current parameterization, and identify the normal gradient as a complementary component with a local descent interpretation. • We propose GDLoRA , which retains standard AdamW optimization of the LoRA factors and applies the token-normalized normal gradient directly to the base weights, without introducing additional base-weight momentum or variance buffers.

Subsequent variants improve initialization, optimization, and adaptation capability. PiSSA ( Meng et al., 2024 ) initializes LoRA using principal singular components of pretrained weights. LoRA-GA ( Wang et al., 2024 ) aligns initial LoRA-induced gradients with full fine-tuning gradients, while LoRA-One ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) studies the relationship between LoRA adapters and full-gradient subspaces. LoRA+ ( Hayou et al., 2024 ) assigns different learning rates to the two factors, and rsLoRA ( Kalajdzievski, 2023 ) uses rank-dependent scaling to stabilize training. AdaLoRA ( Zhang et al., 2023 ) dynamically allocates rank budgets across layers. DoRA ( Liu et al., 2024 ) decomposes weights into magnitude and direction, while LoRA-Pro ( Wang et al., 2025 ) adjusts adapter gradients to better approximate full weight gradients. GaLore ( Zhao et al., 2024 ) reduces optimizer-state memory via low-rank gradient projection; Fira ( Chen et al., 2024 ) adds scaled residual updates for full-rank training. Both reuse SVD bases, trading subspace alignment against refresh costs. GDLoRA instead retains standard LoRA optimization and derives projection bases from the current adapters each step, updating base weights along the normal gradient without full-gradient SVD.

We presented GDLoRA, which complements standard LoRA with gradient information beyond the first-order directions accessible through its current parameterization. Under matched adapter and optimizer configurations, GDLoRA preserves LoRA’s optimizer-state memory budget. Experiments on natural language understanding, mathematical reasoning, commonsense reasoning, and image classification demonstrate consistent improvements over LoRA and a reduced performance gap to FFT. Ablation studies further support the effectiveness of normal-gradient updates in complementing low-rank adaptation.

passages.text: Recent successes of matrix- and curvature-based optimizers have renewed interest in how update geometry shapes learning. These methods normalize or precondition updates, changing how different components progress during training. In deep matrix factorization, the geometry that slows gradient descent (GD) favors low-rank solutions by delaying the emergence of small singular modes. This raises the question of what remains of that spectral bias when normalization or curvature correction weakens or removes the slowdown. We study how optimizer geometry and depth jointly govern this behavior through a common framework for singular mode dynamics. Under explicit balance and alignment assumptions, we derive birth, saturation, and decay laws for Euclidean GD, coordinate-wise updates of SignGD and an instantaneous Adam approximation, spectral updates of Muon and cumulative Shampoo, and a block curvature model of K-FAC. The resulting picture is not a simple ordering from stronger to weaker low-rank bias. To highlight, SignGD and ideal Muon eliminate the divergent birth barrier and drive unsupported modes to zero in finite time. Cumulative Shampoo initially retains GD’s depth-dependent barrier, then accumulated gradients produce a catch-up phase while making previously active modes increasingly persistent. Undamped K-FAC cancels the factorization-induced slowdown while preserving the ordering of the target singular values, whereas positive damping introduces a spectral threshold below which the slow GD phase laws reappear. These results give normalization, accumulated state, damping, and depth a direct interpretation as controls determining when modes emerge, persist, and disappear during training.

Analyses of gradient flow and gradient descent connect spectral dynamics to low rank recovery and incremental rank growth under specified initialization and measurement assumptions ( Gunasekar et al., 2017 ; Arora et al., 2019 ; Li et al., 2021 ; Jin et al., 2023 ) . While depth strengthens the tendency of low rank bias, it is not always equivalent to minimizing a single Schatten norm, indicating that trajectory-level geometry is essential ( Razin and Cohen, 2020 ) . Recent Muon analyses characterize how polar normalization changes spectral learning and simplicity bias in deep linear networks and linear attention ( Dragutinović and Ranganath, 2026 ) , and establish approximately uniform singular value growth under assumptions on LoRA factorization ( Kang et al., 2026 ) . For fully observed bilinear matrix factorization, Rhee et al. (2026) derive uniform factor singular value growth after alignment, and analyze oscillations caused by finite optimization steps. Complementary empirical comparisons show that Muon’s relative performance depends on the factorization problem and hyperparameter tuning ( Parviz et al., 2026 ) . Shampoo has been interpreted as an adapted version of spectral descent that retains information about stochasticity and the parameter trajectory ( Eschenhagen et al., 2026 ) . Building on these results, we compare mode birth, decay, and saturation within a common balanced aligned model. While most analyses study one optimizer in isolation, our analysis includes SignGD and simplified Adam, derives an exact accumulator identity for cumulative Shampoo, and quantifies the effect of additive damping in K-FAC. We give a broader discussion on related works in App. A .

Our analysis shows that the spectral bias of depth depends on optimizer geometry and the stage of training. A surprising consequence is that rapid learning of weak components can coexist with rapid removal of unsupported ones, as illustrated by the Muon analysis. Conversely, accumulated history can accelerate the emergence of a mode while prolonging its persistence. These effects make a single ordering of optimizers by stronger or weaker low-rank bias inadequate. A further implication is that parameters associated with numerical stability also shape learning bias. In the analyzed models, Adam’s stabilizer, Shampoo’s accumulator initialization, and K-FAC’s damping determine where normalization, history, or curvature correction governs spectral progress. They can therefore change how strongly depth suppresses small modes, even within the same optimizer. Although the phase laws rely on balance and alignment assumptions, they identify concrete mechanisms to understand optimizer behavior. This perspective motivates evaluating optimizers through which components they accelerate, suppress, or preserve alongside the training loss, since comparable fit can conceal differences in their dynamics. The resulting framework provides a basis for understanding and testing how faster optimizers change the complexity of intermediate models.

(2026) interpret Shampoo as spectral descent adapted to stochasticity and the parameter trajectory. History dependence is therefore an established feature of this geometry. Our contribution is the exact first integral of the specified cumulative accumulator in the aligned factorization model and its consequences for phase times. That identity does not extend unchanged to exponential averages or different inverse powers. Kerekes et al. (2021) explicitly study natural gradient implicit bias in deep linear classification and matrix factorization. Under their Gaussian model and Jacobian rank condition, natural gradient flow for matrix completion matches direct optimization of the effective matrix, leaving unobserved entries unchanged. This is a direct precedent for connecting geometry to motion outside the observed coordinates. Our block curvature analysis quantifies the effect of additive damping on mode birth and decay, and distinguishes it from both full curvature and factored damping. These works provide important geometry and momentum precedents, while our phase laws concern squared loss, explicit stabilization or damping factors, and finite targets in factorized models.

Fig. 4 provides a broader validation of the theory in addition to the theoretical evaluation done in Sec. 6 . Fig. 5 compares the optimization and rank dynamics. GD learns the target modes sequentially and retains a low effective rank for longer, consistent with the small mode mobility factor σ p \sigma^{p} . Adam reduces this separation and activates weaker modes much earlier. Muon produces an even more rapid redistribution of spectral mass, reflecting its normalized spectral update. Cumulative Shampoo initially behaves more like GD but quickly changes regime as its accumulated preconditioner adapts. K-FAC exhibits a smoother evolution in which curvature correction reduces the factorization induced separation between mode time scales. passages.text: We propose a novel optimizer for low-rank adaptation (LoRA) that explicitly incorporates the gauge symmetry of low-rank factorization. Our optimizer extends recent matrix optimizers for full-parameter training to the manifold of fixed-rank matrices by interpreting them as normalization under a rotated basis. We show how rotation and normalization can be integrated with the fixed-rank manifold efficiently. Our optimizer converges faster to lower held-out loss and achieves better or comparable downstream performance on both supervised finetuning and reinforcement learning tasks.

Large language models (LLMs) based on the transformer architecture ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ) have achieved remarkable success in recent years ( Brown et al., 2020 ; Touvron et al., 2023 ; Guo et al., 2025 ) . These models typically adopt a pretraining-finetuning paradigm, where large-scale pretraining equips a model with general capabilities and subsequent finetuning adapts it to specific downstream applications. However, as LLMs grow to billions of parameters, full-parameter finetuning becomes expensive in both computation and memory. Such a challenge has motivated the development of parameter-efficient finetuning (PEFT) methods ( Houlsby et al., 2019 ) , which only update a small fraction of all parameters. Among these approaches, low-rank adaptation (LoRA) ( Hu et al., 2022 ) has emerged as a particularly effective method and has been widely adopted. LoRA freezes the pretrained weights and parametrizes the weight updates as products of low-rank matrices, substantially reducing the number of trainable parameters and the memory footprint, while maintaining competitive performance. Compared with full-parameter training, LoRA exhibits a unique geometric structure induced by its low-rank factorization. Specifically, the low-rank matrices have infinitely many reparameterizations that represent the same weight update, since the model’s output depends on these low-rank factors only through their product. This invariance, commonly referred to as gauge symmetry, suggests that optimization should respect the underlying geometry of the weight space of the LoRA parametrization. Motivated by this observation, we revisit the optimization of LoRA and aim to explicitly incorporate its gauge symmetry into the design of the optimization algorithm.

We design our optimizer on the manifold of fixed-rank matrices, aiming to optimize the product of the low-rank factors directly rather than each factor separately. We extend the recent advances in matrix optimizers ( Gong et al., 2026 ; Jordan et al., 2024 ; Vyas et al., 2025 ) to the fixed-rank manifold by interpreting their update rules as normalization under a rotated basis. Our optimizer applies row and column normalization in a conditioning frame defined by the left singular vectors of the tangent momentum, projects the resulting direction back onto the tangent space, and retracts to the fixed-rank manifold. By exploiting the low-rank structure of tangent vectors, all operations can be performed using thin factors without materializing full weight-sized matrices. We refer to our proposed optimizer as RoM ( Ro tated M anifold Optimization). We evaluate RoM on supervised finetuning and reinforcement learning tasks. RoM achieves substantially lower held-out loss and better or comparable downstream task performance compared with other LoRA optimizers, with only modest additional computational overhead.

We further evaluate RoM on LoRA-based RL finetuning using the VeRL framework ( Sheng et al., 2025 ) . Since the other LoRA baselines do not specify an RL training recipe, we focus on comparing RoM against Adam. We train the Qwen2.5-3B base model ( Yang et al., 2024 ) using GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) on the training split of MATH (7.5K problems) with rank r = 16 r=16 . At each rollout step, we sample 8 responses for each of 128 prompts, yielding 1024 sequences per optimization step. We use no KL penalty and train for 400 steps. Following the setup of Liu et al. (2025) , we use the bare questions as prompts with no chat template. We evaluate the finetuned model using greedy decoding on three held-out benchmarks: MATH-500 (500 examples), GSM8K test (1319 examples), and OlympiadBench ( He et al., 2024 ) (674 examples). We tune Adam’s learning rate on a logarithmic grid and select 3 × 10 − 6 3\times 10^{-6} . We use the same learning rate for RoM without further tuning. Results are mean ± \pm standard deviation. “Time” denotes the median end-to-end wall clock time per optimizer step, normalized to Adam. Figure 2 shows evaluation accuracy on the three held-out benchmarks throughout RL finetuning. RoM improves accuracy faster than Adam and reaches higher final accuracy on all three benchmarks. Table 4 reports the final evaluation results over three independent runs. Unlike in SFT, where downstream differences among optimizers are relatively small, RoM shows a clearer advantage over Adam in RL finetuning, while requiring only 1.08 × 1.08\times the per-step training time on 4 NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPUs.

We presented RoM, a manifold-based optimizer for LoRA that directly optimizes the fixed-rank weight adaptation while avoiding the redundancy of factorized parameterizations. By exploiting the low-rank structure of tangent vectors, RoM enables efficient Riemannian optimization with memory requirement comparable to conventional LoRA optimization. Across supervised finetuning and reinforcement learning experiments, RoM consistently achieves lower validation loss than existing LoRA optimizers, while also improving downstream performance in the RL setting. Ablation experiments further show that both normalization and rotation contribute to its optimization performance.

papers.relevance: Directly addresses optimization of frozen-backbone low-rank factors and practical language-model fine-tuning.

evidence.quote: We design our optimizer on the manifold of fixed-rank matrices, aiming to optimize the product of the low-rank factors directly rather than each factor separately.

Unlike in SFT, where downstream differences among optimizers are relatively small, RoM shows a clearer advantage over Adam in RL finetuning, while requiring only 1.08 × 1.08\times the per-step training time on 4 NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPUs.

limitations: The Ori memory numbers measure additional peak memory during optimizer.step(), not total peak training memory.
BMuon's highlighted compression result is structured MLP-channel pruning on ViT-S/16, not low-rank compression of LLM weights.
CORE's reported comparisons use closed-search benchmarks, not a paper-digest evaluation.
Idea2Prior's historical comparison includes a convention-based ChatGPT hit and does not establish contamination-free or statistically general superiority.
The retrieved RoM passages do not quantify supervised fine-tuning gains or peak memory; its reported RL time cost should not be generalized to other settings.
X analysis was disabled; no attention inference was used.
